title: Twelve chairs, forty patients
note: Fictional unit and patients. DRAFT pending clinical sign-off. Your unit protocol, the attending nephrologist and your local disaster authorities decide every real event.
intro: You are the head nurse of a 20-station unit in Tacloban, two days after a typhoon. The unit can run 12 chairs for one long shift. Forty patients are due. Two receiving units (Ormoc and Palo) can take six each tomorrow. The tracking board: 31 reached, 4 dialyzed at a hospital, 5 not reached.

choices.text: Give the attending nephrologist each reached patient’s time since last treatment, last potassium, fluid status and symptoms; the nephrologist sets the priority roster.
choices.feedback: Priority is a medical decision; your job is the facts.

choices.text: First come, first served at the door.
choices.feedback: Arrival order is not medical need; the patient with a potassium of 6.9 could wait behind someone stable.
choices.then: The physician-on-duty stops the queue and calls the nephrologist.

choices.text: You choose the 12 yourself, based on who seems sickest.
choices.feedback: Your observations help, but the decision belongs to the nephrologist.
choices.then: The nephrologist reviews your list and changes three names.

n2.scene: The Dialysis Clinical Head suggests shortening sessions to fit more patients today.

choices.text: All six conditions: the shortage recorded by the Dialysis Clinical Head, a written nephrologist order per patient or group, an end or review date, high-risk patients (the man with potassium 6.9, the breathless woman) excluded, potassium and fluid monitored, and a recorded return to full sessions.
choices.feedback: Shortened sessions are a conditional option, used only when all six hold.

choices.text: Shorten everyone by 90 minutes, including the high-potassium and breathless patients, to fit 16.
choices.feedback: High-risk patients keep full sessions or move first to a receiving unit.
choices.then: The nephrologist cancels it and writes an order for three stable patients only.

choices.text: Never shorten; send everyone beyond 12 home with the diet sheet.
choices.feedback: Shortening is not required, but refusing every option may leave overdue patients waiting days.
choices.then: The nephrologist decides on three shortened sessions with an order.

n3.prompt: How are 12 patients sent to Ormoc and Palo tomorrow?

choices.text: Confirm the accepting person at each unit by name, send each patient’s handoff (prescription, access type and side, last laboratory results with hepatitis status, medicines, allergies, dry weight), arrange safe transport, and record each placement on the board.
choices.feedback: A receiving unit can dialyze safely only with the facts and only if it expects the patient.

choices.text: Text each unit the patients’ names and send them.
choices.feedback: Without a handoff, the receiving unit must guess the prescription and hepatitis status.
choices.then: Palo calls back asking for prescriptions; you send full handoffs.

n4.scene: Five patients are still not reached after 24 hours.

choices.text: Keep them on the board; tell the incident lead and the attending nephrologist; ask the social worker, barangay health workers and the LDRRMO to help find them.
choices.feedback: A patient not reached may be in danger.

choices.text: Mark them as “probably dialyzed elsewhere” and close the board.
choices.then: A week later one arrives at the hospital with severe hyperkalemia.

end.title: Day 3
end.text: Fifteen patients dialyzed by the nephrologist’s roster, twelve placed with handoffs, and three of five missing patients found; the search continues for two.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • The nephrologist sets the priority roster from time since treatment, potassium, fluid and symptoms.
  • Shortened sessions need all six conditions, and high-risk patients are excluded.
  • Every placement needs a named accepting person and a handoff; no patient leaves the board until found.
